desc:
Given integers n, r and a prime p, return the binomial coefficient C(n, r) (the number of ways to choose r items from n) modulo p.

Here n can be as large as about two billion while p is a small prime (at most 1,000), so n may be far larger than p and the usual shortcut with factorials fails, because n! is divisible by p.

n = 5, r = 2, p = 7        -> C(5,2) = 10 -> 3
n = 10, r = 5, p = 3       -> C(10,5) = 252 -> 0
n = 2000000000, r = 3, p = 2 -> 0
constraints: p is a prime with 2 ≤ p ≤ 1,000
hints: If n < p, the answer is n! / (r! (n-r)!) computed with modular inverses (Fermat: x-1 = xp-2 mod p). What breaks when n ≥ p?
Write n and r in base p. Lucas' theorem says C(n, r) is congruent modulo p to the product of C(ni, ri) over corresponding base-p digits.
Precompute factorials modulo p up to p - 1. For each pair of digits, return 0 as soon as ri > ni; otherwise multiply in the small binomial computed with factorials and inverse factorials.
editorial: Lucas' theorem: if n = nkpk + ... + n0 and r = rkpk + ... + r0 in base p, then C(n, r) ≡ ∏ C(ni, ri) (mod p), where C(a, b) = 0 if b > a. Each digit is below p, so each small binomial can be evaluated with factorials mod p without any factor of p appearing.

Precompute fact[0..p-1] mod p. A small binomial is fact[a] * inv(fact[b]) * inv(fact[a-b]) mod p, where the inverse of x is xp-2 mod p by Fermat's little theorem (all values involved are non-zero modulo p since they are below p).

The loop runs once per base-p digit, at most 31 times (for p = 2), and each step costs a logarithmic modular power. Setup is O(p). Early exit on a zero result is a nice optimization: it happens exactly when some digit of r exceeds the corresponding digit of n.
